Why, that gives us the makings of a wonderfully spooky superstition. I suppose you will name the beetle scarabæus caput hominis, or something similar—natural history books contain plenty of names like that. But where are the antennae you mentioned?”

“The antennae!” Legrand said, becoming strangely heated over the matter. “Surely you can see them. I drew them just as clearly as they appear on the actual insect, and I should think that is enough.”

“Well, well,” I answered, “perhaps you did, but I still cannot see them.” I returned the paper without further comment, unwilling to upset him. Yet this turn in the conversation surprised me greatly. His irritation was puzzling, and there were certainly no visible antennae in the drawing. The picture really did look remarkably like an ordinary illustration of a skull.

He took the paper back crossly and seemed about to crumple it up and throw it into the fire. Then a chance glance at the drawing suddenly caught his attention. His face flushed bright red, and a moment later turned just as pale. For several minutes he sat studying the picture closely. At last he got up, took a candle from the table, and moved to a sea chest in the farthest corner of the room. Sitting there, he examined the paper anxiously again, turning it this way and that. He said nothing. His behaviour astonished me, but I thought it wise not to make his growing moodiness worse by commenting. Soon he took a wallet from his coat pocket, carefully slipped the paper inside, and locked both away in a writing desk. He now seemed calmer, though his earlier excitement had completely vanished. Still, he appeared distracted rather than sulky. As the evening passed, he became increasingly lost in thought, and none of my lively remarks could draw him out. I had planned to spend the night at the hut, as I often had before. But seeing my host in this state, I decided it would be better to leave. He did not urge me to stay, though he shook my hand more warmly than usual when I said goodbye.

About a month later, during which time I had not seen Legrand at all, his servant Jupiter came to visit me in Charleston. I had never seen the good old Black man looking so unhappy. I became afraid that some terrible misfortune had happened to my friend.

At noon on Saturday I went over to the well and watched for a time. Merlin was still setting off smoke-powders, clutching at the air, and mumbling nonsense as vigorously as ever, though he looked decidedly discouraged; naturally, he had not yet coaxed so much as a sweat from the well. At last I asked:

‘How are the prospects looking now, partner?’

‘Behold, I am at this very moment trying the mightiest enchantment known to the masters of occult learning in the Eastern lands. Should this fail, nothing can serve. Be silent until I have done.’

This time he produced smoke enough to blacken the whole neighbourhood. It must have been unpleasant for the hermits, since the wind blew toward them and sent it rolling over their retreats in thick, swelling clouds. His torrents of words kept pace with it, while he twisted himself about and chopped at the air with his hands in the most astonishing fashion. After twenty minutes he sank down, gasping and nearly spent. The abbot now appeared with several hundred monks and nuns, followed by a crowd of pilgrims and a couple of acres’ worth of foundlings, all attracted by the tremendous smoke and all wildly excited. The abbot anxiously asked what had been accomplished. Merlin replied:

‘If any mortal labour could undo the charm imprisoning these waters, the effort I have just made would have undone it. It has failed. Thus I know that my former fear is proved: this failure signifies that the strongest spirit known to Eastern magicians, whose name no man can pronounce and live, has enchanted the well. No mortal now breathes, nor ever shall, who can discover the secret of that charm; and without its secret it cannot be broken. Good Father, these waters shall flow no more for all eternity. I have performed all that man may do. Permit me to depart.’

Naturally, this filled the abbot with considerable dismay. He turned his troubled face toward me and asked:

‘Ye have heard his words. Are they true?’

‘Some of them.’

‘Then not all, not all! Which part is true?’

‘That the spirit with the Russian name has bewitched the well.’

‘God’s wounds! Then we are lost!’

‘Perhaps.’

‘But not assuredly? Ye mean it is not assured?’

‘Precisely.’

‘Then ye likewise mean that when he declares no one can break the spell—’

‘Yes; that statement is not necessarily correct. Under certain conditions, an attempt to undo it might stand a chance—some slight, quite insignificant chance, that is—of succeeding.’

Before him, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man of fearsome appearance. His eyes glowed like live red coals; long grey locks hung in tangled masses about his shoulders; his old-fashioned clothes were filthy and torn, and heavy handcuffs and rusted fetters dangled from his wrists and ankles.

‘My dear fellow,’ Mr. Otis said, ‘I must really ask you to oil those chains. To assist you, I have brought a little bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. A single application is said to produce a complete effect, and you will find several endorsements on the wrapper from some of our most distinguished American clergymen. I shall put it here beside the bedroom candles, and will gladly furnish another supply if you need it.’ Having said this, the United States Minister set the bottle upon a marble table, shut his door, and went back to bed.

For an instant the Canterville ghost remained utterly still, filled with understandable outrage. Then he hurled the bottle onto the shining floor and rushed along the corridor, groaning hollowly and giving off a dreadful green radiance. But just as he came to the head of the great oak stairs, a door flew open. Two small figures in white robes appeared, and a large pillow shot past his head. Clearly there was not a moment to spare. Hastily resorting to the Fourth Dimension of Space for his escape, he disappeared through the wood panelling, and silence returned to the house.

When he arrived at a little hidden chamber in the left wing, he rested against a moonbeam to regain his breath and attempted to grasp his situation. Throughout an illustrious and unbroken career of three centuries, he had never suffered so outrageous an affront. He recalled the Dowager Duchess, whom he had terrified into a fit while she stood at her mirror wearing lace and diamonds; the four housemaids who had fallen into hysterics at no more than his grin from behind the curtains in a spare bedroom; and the parish rector, whose candle he had extinguished one late night as the man left the library, and who had ever since been a patient of Sir William Gull, suffering cruelly from nervous complaints. Then there was old Madame de Tremouillac. Waking early one morning to discover a skeleton sitting in an armchair by the hearth and reading her diary, she had taken to her bed for six weeks with brain fever. Upon recovering, she had made her peace with the Church and severed her relations with the celebrated sceptic Monsieur de Voltaire.
